static.topic: Intermediary Liability and the IT Rules, 2021
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Government Policies and Interventions; Polity — Fundamental Rights
static.whatIsIt: Intermediaries are platforms that host third-party content. Under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 they enjoy 'safe harbour' — exemption from liability for user content — only if they observe due diligence conditions prescribed by the government, which are set out in the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.
static.background: Section 79 safe harbour and the blocking power under Section 69A were tested in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), where the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A but upheld Section 69A with procedural safeguards. The IT Rules, 2021 were notified in February 2021, introducing grievance officers, timelines for takedown on complaint, and additional duties for 'significant social media intermediaries' above a user threshold. Amendments in 2022 created Grievance Appellate Committees, and further changes in 2023 addressed online gaming.
static.socioEconomic: Compliance costs and takedown obligations disproportionately affect small Indian platforms, while large foreign platforms absorb them — a point raised in debates on platform neutrality and the level playing field.
static.whyInNews: Meta's decision to withhold posts about a political memoir 'citing legal requirements' is precisely the kind of opaque, statute-referencing enforcement that the safe-harbour and blocking framework enables.
static.wayForward: Move from opaque compliance claims to reasoned, auditable takedown orders with mandatory disclosure to the affected user, time-bound appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee, and periodic transparency reporting by platforms disaggregated by ground of removal.
prelimsPointers: Safe harbour for intermediaries flows from Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 and is conditional on due diligence.
The IT Rules, 2021 impose a 36-hour takedown timeline on receipt of a court or government order, with shorter timelines for certain categories.
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act while upholding Section 69A.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's intermediary liability regime, as operationalised by the IT Rules, 2021, adequately protects free expression while ensuring platform accountability.

static.topic: Freedom of Speech and Expression: Article 19(1)(a) and Its Limits
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights (Article 19)
static.whatIsIt: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees every citizen the right to freedom of speech and expression. It is not absolute: Article 19(2) permits the State to impose reasonable restrictions on specified grounds, and restrictions must be by law, proportionate, and narrowly drawn.
static.background: The original Article 19(2) grounds were widened by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, which added public order, friendly relations with foreign states and incitement to an offence. The Supreme Court has since read in proportionality, and in Shreya Singhal (2015) held that speech can be restricted only under a law falling within Article 19(2). Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) held that indefinite internet suspension is impermissible and that orders must be published and subject to review.
static.socioEconomic: Online speech restrictions bear unevenly on journalists, activists and regional-language users, raising questions of a chilling effect on political discourse.
static.whyInNews: Withholding of posts about a political memoir, and large-scale state police takedowns, both implicate Article 19(1)(a) and the permissible scope of restrictions on political speech.
static.wayForward: Codify proportionality in takedown practice, require reasoned and published orders, guarantee pre-decisional notice and post-decisional appeal to the speaker, and treat content removal as a last resort after less restrictive measures.
prelimsPointers: Article 19(2) grounds include sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.
Article 19 rights are available to citizens, not to non-citizens or (for speech) to corporations in the same way.
Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A as vague and overbroad.
static.mainsAngle: How far does the constitutional test of 'reasonableness' constrain private platforms acting at the State's behest? Discuss with reference to political speech online.

static.topic: Platform Accountability, Misinformation and Cyber Policing
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Cyber Security and Social Media; Science and Technology — Information Technology
static.whatIsIt: Content moderation sits at the intersection of platform design, algorithmic amplification and police action on online complaints. Misinformation (false content shared without intent to harm) and disinformation (deliberately created false content) are countered through a mix of statutory powers, platform policy and cyber-crime policing.
static.background: The IT Act, 2000 provides the core legal architecture; the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) under the Ministry of Home Affairs coordinates cyber-crime response, and CERT-In issues directions for cyber security incidents and log retention. State police cyber wings handle complaints and takedown requests. The proposed Digital India Act is intended to eventually replace the IT Act framework.
static.socioEconomic: Takedown regimes impose indirect costs on creators and regional-language users, while misinformation during elections and communal flashpoints carries wider social cost.
static.whyInNews: Kerala Police's disclosure of 15,627 removed posts, alongside Meta's algorithmic retuning in India and its withholding of memoir-related content, illustrates the three-way traffic among platforms, police and users.
static.wayForward: Publish disaggregated takedown statistics, route all removal requests through a documented legal order, invest in independent fact-checking and media literacy, and adopt algorithmic transparency and risk-assessment obligations for large platforms.
prelimsPointers: CERT-In is the national nodal agency for responding to cyber security incidents, functioning under MeitY.
I4C is the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre set up under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The IT Act, 2000 is the principal statute governing online content and intermediary obligations in India.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the balance between state policing of online content and platform self-regulation in India; suggest safeguards that preserve both public order and free expression.

prelims: Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads, and is therefore a 'significant social media intermediary' under the IT Rules, 2021.
Kerala Police reported removal of 15,627 social media posts since the UDF government came to power in the state.
Meta stated that it retuned Instagram's recommendation systems in India to reduce suggestive and violent content.
Takedown of online content by the government is exercised under Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, with procedural safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015).
stories.mainsQuestion: Platforms increasingly cite 'legal requirements' to withhold political content in India. Examine how the intermediary liability framework and Article 19 jurisprudence together shape who decides what remains visible online, and suggest safeguards to make such decisions transparent and appealable.

static.topic: Securities Market Regulation and Leverage in India
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Capital Markets / Financial Sector Regulation
static.whatIsIt: SEBI is the statutory regulator of India's securities market, with quasi-legislative, executive and judicial powers. Leverage means taking equity exposure with borrowed money — through margin trading, margin intraday products or derivatives — which magnifies both gains and losses and can amplify market-wide volatility.
static.background: SEBI was constituted in 1988 and given statutory backing by the SEBI Act, 1992; it is headquartered in Mumbai. Over time it has tightened the margin architecture, notably through the peak-margin framework rolled out in phases from December 2020, which requires upfront collection of margins. The BSE (established 1875) and the NSE (1992) are the principal exchanges.
static.geography: SEBI is headquartered in Mumbai, alongside the BSE and NSE — India's two main equity exchanges.
static.socioEconomic: Retail participation has broadened sharply since 2020, with a large share of first-time, younger investors; losses on leveraged and derivative positions therefore carry household-level financial-stability and investor-protection implications.
static.whyInNews: A Reuters exclusive reports that India may restrict leveraged stock bets to curb volatility, reviving the debate over how tightly retail speculation should be regulated.
static.wayForward: Calibrated and well-sequenced curbs rather than abrupt changes, backed by risk-based supervision and investor education; stability of the rule-book matters as much as the rule itself.
prelimsPointers: SEBI became a statutory body under the SEBI Act, 1992; its headquarters is in Mumbai.
Margin trading allows investors to buy securities with borrowed funds, magnifying both profit and loss.
Peak margin norms, introduced in phases from December 2020, require full upfront margin collection by brokers.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether tightening leverage norms is an effective macroprudential answer to retail speculation, and how the regulator should balance investor protection against market depth and ease of participation.

static.topic: Fiscal Policy, Budget and FRBM
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Government Budgeting
static.whatIsIt: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation and spending to steer the economy, presented annually through the Union Budget (Article 112). Fiscal prudence is anchored by the FRBM Act, 2003.
static.background: The FRBM Act targets fiscal-deficit reduction; the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor of 60% for general government. The GST Council (Article 279A) is the constitutional body for indirect-tax harmonisation, with GST launched in 2017.

stories.headline: Bangladesh: nuclear grid link, garment unrest, Hasina return row
stories.summary: Bangladesh has connected its first nuclear power plant to the national grid, a step aimed at easing a fuel crisis aggravated by conflict in West Asia. At the same time, garment workers blocked key highways—Dhaka-Aricha, Dhaka-Tangail and Dhaka-Mymensingh—demanding higher wages, prompting police and paramilitary personnel to use tear gas, sound grenades and batons. The labour unrest coincides with a nearly 12% fall in Bangladesh’s apparel exports to the EU over a nine-month period, a loss of about €1.82 billion, with China gaining market share. Politically, an adviser to Bangladesh’s Prime Minister said India cannot dictate the terms of Sheikh Hasina’s return; Hasina has been in India since fleeing in August 2024 after a student-led uprising toppled her government.

static.topic: Judicial review, contempt jurisdiction and the courts–politics interface
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Structure, organisation and functioning of the Judiciary; judicial review
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution. Both the Supreme Court and High Courts are courts of record with the power to punish for contempt.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 (Supreme Court) and 226 (High Courts) provide writ jurisdiction, and Article 142 gives the Supreme Court wide power to do complete justice.
static.socioEconomic: Judicial backlog, high pendency and vacancies shape access to justice; contempt proceedings against elected representatives raise questions about institutional balance between the judiciary and the political executive.
static.whyInNews: On 17 November 2026, the Supreme Court's reconsideration of the two-child norm, a Delhi High Court contempt case involving Kejriwal and other AAP leaders, a Supreme Court caution to Sanjay Raut on restraint, a Rajasthan High Court order on censor clearance for an online release, and a Karnataka High Court order in a substandard-medicines prosecution all featured in the day's legal news.
static.wayForward: Reduce judicial vacancies and pendency through case-management reforms; keep contempt jurisdiction confined to wilful disobedience or scandalising the court; and maintain clarity on judicial restraint in matters of policy.

static.wayForward: Resolve ritual-rights disputes through evidence-based findings on custom, and balance religious freedom, state neutrality and heritage conservation.

static.wayForward: Any population-linked eligibility norm should be assessed against reproductive autonomy, equality before law and the voluntary, rights-based approach of the National Population Policy, 2000.

static.topic: Exported emissions and the production-versus-consumption accounting debate

static.whatIsIt: Exported CO2 emissions are emissions released within a country to produce goods and services consumed elsewhere; attributing them to the exporter rather than the consumer changes the picture of historical responsibility.
static.background: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle; Paris relies on NDCs and a ratchet mechanism, and the Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030, and leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission.
static.socioEconomic: Export-led manufacturing economies, including India, argue that consumption-based accounting would shift mitigation obligations towards importing countries and that carbon border measures penalise their producers.
static.whyInNews: Carbon Brief reported that Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest historical exporters of CO2 emissions, reviving the production-versus-consumption accounting debate.
static.wayForward: Strengthen Article 6 carbon market rules and transparency so exported emissions become visible, and press for climate finance and technology transfer in the follow-up to the Global Stocktake.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
Loss & Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023).
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether consumption-based emissions accounting should supplement territorial accounting, and what it implies for equity and India's climate diplomacy.

stories.headline: AI climate denial, Voyager 1's Morse call, cancer vaccine: science briefs
stories.summary: A clutch of science, health and technology developments dominated the day. A UNESCO–UCL report found that leading AI models readily abandon established climate facts when users push back, sharpening concerns about AI-amplified misinformation. NASA marked Voyager 1's approach to roughly a one-light-day distance from Earth — about 24 hours of one-way signal travel — by asking the public to flash 'VGR' in Morse code. In biotech, Sellas reported that its vaccine extended survival in a blood cancer trial, while Alphabet-backed Isomorphic Labs raised $5 billion to push AI-designed drugs towards clinical trials. Indian commentary focused on health-system reform — pairing frontline experience with operational research, pushing back on exaggerated fake-drug fears (the 2017 National Drug Survey found counterfeit drugs at 0.0245%), and arguing that water and sanitation are the real last mile in disease elimination — alongside AI's role in education and the case for gender-sensitive disaster response.
stories.whyItMatters: The brief spans GS-III science and technology, environment and health, and GS-II global governance — testing how AI, space missions and biomedical innovation are reshaping policy, regulation and public trust. It also supplies ready prelims facts on AI ethics, drug quality data and India's climate commitments.

perspectives.take: Three op-eds converge on health-system reform: frontline workers should co-design operational research, fake-drug panic is disproportionate (2017 National Drug Survey: 0.0245% counterfeit), and safe water and sanitation are the true last mile in disease elimination — a reformist, India-centric establishment view.

stories.headline: India's rice dominance strains water, farmers and global markets
stories.summary: India has grown into the world's largest rice exporter, a position built over decades through the Green Revolution, assured MSP-backed paddy procurement, subsidised power and irrigation, and large public stocks held by the Food Corporation of India. That success now carries mounting costs at home: paddy is among the most water-intensive staple crops, and its concentration in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh has contributed to declining water tables, soil stress and an increasingly skewed cropping pattern. At the same time, export restrictions and stockholding decisions taken to shield domestic consumers have tightened global rice availability and added to price volatility, pushing importing countries to diversify their suppliers. The Reuters report frames the dilemma as one in which India's food-security architecture simultaneously underwrites world supply and strains its own natural resource base.
stories.whyItMatters: It ties together three recurring UPSC themes — MSP and procurement reform, agricultural export policy, and groundwater sustainability — showing how food security, farmer incomes and resource conservation pull in different directions.

perspectives.take: A global newswire, market-access lens: frames India's rice rise as an export-policy and commodity-market story, stressing how domestic subsidies, procurement and export curbs ripple through world prices and import-dependent economies.

static.topic: MSP, Procurement and Food Security
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture & Food Security
static.whatIsIt: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is a price assurance announced by the government on the recommendations of the CACP for 22 mandated crops. It operates alongside the National Food Security Act, 2013, and PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana grain distribution, with the FCI handling procurement and buffer stocking — mainly of wheat and paddy.
static.background: The Green Revolution of the 1960s made India food-sufficient but locked the procurement system into wheat and paddy. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations and recommended reforms. PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 per year as income support. The three farm laws of 2020 were repealed in 2021, leaving the MSP-procurement debate unresolved.
static.geography: Procurement and paddy concentration is heaviest in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, with expanding acreage in Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal.
static.socioEconomic: Assured procurement underwrites farm incomes and rural stability but also encourages water-intensive cropping, distorts cropping patterns and generates large carrying costs for public granaries.
static.whyInNews: India's scale as the world's leading rice exporter has renewed scrutiny of how MSP, subsidies and export restrictions together shape both domestic resources and global markets.
static.wayForward: Diversify procurement beyond wheat and paddy, link support to crop diversification and water use, strengthen e-NAM and warehouse infrastructure, and shift from price support to income and investment support.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement remains concentrated in wheat and paddy.
NFSA covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
static.mainsAngle: Reforming MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes and safeguarding water and soil sustainability.

static.topic: Water-Intensive Cropping and Groundwater Stress
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Conservation, Groundwater & Sustainable Agriculture
static.whatIsIt: Paddy cultivation is highly water-intensive, and its expansion onto assured-irrigation tracts has made groundwater the principal source of irrigation in north-western India, leading to falling water tables in several assessment units.
static.background: The Central Ground Water Board classifies assessment units as safe, semi-critical, critical or over-exploited, and a substantial share of blocks in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh fall in the stressed categories. Policy responses include the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana with its 'Per Drop More Crop' micro-irrigation component and the community-led Atal Bhujal Yojana for water-stressed areas.
static.geography: Indo-Gangetic plains — Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, and parts of Rajasthan — where paddy-wheat rotation dominates the cropping cycle.
static.socioEconomic: Subsidised or free farm power for tube wells lowers the private cost of pumping, encourages over-extraction, and shifts the burden of depletion onto future users and the public exchequer.
static.whyInNews: The Reuters report on India's rice dominance highlights how export success is materially sustained by scarce irrigation water and stressed aquifers.
static.wayForward: Crop diversification away from paddy, direct-seeded rice and other water-saving techniques, metering or rationalising farm power subsidies, micro-irrigation, and aquifer-level community management.
prelimsPointers: The Central Ground Water Board categorises assessment units as safe, semi-critical, critical and over-exploited.
Atal Bhujal Yojana is a community-led groundwater management programme focused on water-stressed areas, supported by the World Bank.
static.mainsAngle: How should India reconcile its role as a global food exporter with the long-term sustainability of its aquifers and soil?

static.topic: Tropical Cyclones and the Indian Monsoon
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India
static.whatIsIt: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems that develop over warm ocean waters and can bring heavy rain, strong winds and storm surge to coastal India. The Bay of Bengal is a major cyclone-genesis region.
static.background: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift and the Tibetan Plateau heat pump; it delivers about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September. El Niño usually weakens the monsoon, La Niña strengthens it, and the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it. Cyclones occur in the pre-monsoon and post-monsoon transition seasons, with the post-monsoon Bay of Bengal being particularly active.
static.geography: Bay of Bengal; west-central Bay of Bengal; eastern coast of India; Andhra Pradesh and Odisha coasts; Eastern Ghats; coastal deltas.
static.socioEconomic: Cyclones cause storm surge, flooding, wind damage, crop loss, displacement and loss of livelihoods. Coastal communities, agriculture, fisheries and infrastructure are highly vulnerable.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Akvan is stationary over the west-central Bay of Bengal and is likely to move slowly north-northwestwards, intensifying into a Severe Cyclonic Storm around November 18, 2026.
static.wayForward: Strengthen early warning dissemination, cyclone shelters, evacuation drills, mangrove and coastal ecosystem restoration, and climate-resilient infrastructure.

static.topic: Cyclone Disaster Management in India
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Cyclones
static.whatIsIt: Cyclone disaster management involves forecasting, warning, evacuation, sheltering and post-cyclone relief and rehabilitation. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) is the nodal agency for cyclone warnings and names cyclones under a regional convention.
static.background: India's disaster management framework is anchored in the Disaster Management Act, 2005, which established the NDMA, SDMAs and NDRF. IMD issues colour-coded warnings and tracks cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea. Cyclone naming follows a formula agreed by WMO/ESCAP panel countries.
static.geography: Coastal India, especially the Bay of Bengal coast; Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu are frequently affected.
static.socioEconomic: Effective early warning and evacuation have reduced cyclone mortality, but economic losses and infrastructure damage remain high. Fisheries, agriculture and tourism are disrupted.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Akvan's expected intensification into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal highlights the need for coastal preparedness.
static.wayForward: Invest in last-mile warning connectivity, multi-purpose cyclone shelters, community-based disaster risk reduction, and ecosystem-based coastal protection.
prelimsPointers: The Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2005.
IMD is the nodal agency for cyclone warnings in India.
Cyclone names are contributed by WMO/ESCAP panel countries.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the effectiveness of India's cyclone early warning and evacuation systems in reducing disaster mortality and economic losses.
